title: Video Has No Memory. Here's How We Built One. — James Le, TwelveLabs
talk_summary: TwelveLabs argues video AI needs a persistent 'memory layer' (context graph of moments, entities, appearances, relationships) rather than repeated frame/transcript sampling per query. They describe a 'video worker' harness with planning, retrieval, expert tools, explicit operating envelopes, output contracts, and evaluation.

takeaways.what_they_do: Pay expensive interpretation cost once at ingestion and store reusable representations, instead of re-parsing source data on every request.
Give each worker explicit limits on time, cost, depth, scope, and autonomy so it knows how deep to inspect and when to stop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: explicit limit on time, cost, depth, scope, autonomy

takeaways.what_they_do: Require structured output with references/timestamps rather than free natural language, and ground every claim to a source location.
takeaways.evidence_quote: sometimes the patient needs structured data with references and time stamp

takeaways.what_they_do: Break evaluation into component checks: did retrieval find the right evidence, did synthesis preserve it, did the worker stay in budget.
takeaways.evidence_quote: did the retrieval find the right evidence? Did the synthesis preserve it, right? Did the worker stay within the budget?

takeaways.technique: Context graph of primitives, not answers
takeaways.what_they_do: Store primitives (moments, entities, appearances, relationships) in a navigable graph so different queries traverse different parts, instead of storing only final answers.
The worker first classifies the query (search vs summarization vs multi-step reasoning) and plans the task before selecting evidence.
